source: Wallace and Boulton (1968) An information measure for classification (read via Wikipedia summary)
finding: MML was introduced in a clustering paper. Hypothesis and data are coded as one two-part message. The best hypothesis gives the shortest total message.
numbers: Computer Journal 11(2):185-194. Message split: -log2 P(H&E) = -log2 P(H) + -log2 P(E|H). No effect sizes in the page.
limits: Read via the Wikipedia page, not the 1968 PDF (publisher returned 403). Founding numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: A two-part cost of hypothesis plus data-given-hypothesis is a clean scoring rule for choosing among candidate explanations.

source: Allison, MML overview page (Monash)
finding: MML is Bayesian. It favours explicit priors and fully parameterised models. It is not the same as MAP in general. Every continuous parameter has an optimal finite precision at which it should be stated.
numbers: Cites Wallace and Boulton 1968; Wallace and Freeman 1987 (JRSS B 49(3)); Wallace 2005 book; Allison 2018 book. Models done: binomial, multinomial, normal, regression, von Mises-Fisher, mixtures, HMM, decision trees, Bayesian networks, factor analysis.
limits: Author is an MML insider. Page lists models and gives no comparative scores.
agent_relevance: State claims at a precision the evidence supports. Do not give over-precise estimates.

source: Allison, MML Fisher information page
finding: Derives the Wallace-Freeman approximation. The best stated interval for a parameter has width s with s^2 = 12/F(theta). Message length is about -ln h(theta) - ln f(x|theta) + 0.5 ln F(theta) + a constant.
numbers: Constant is -0.5 ln 12 + 0.5 per parameter. Lattice constant 1/12 for one parameter and 5/(36*sqrt(3)) for two (from the normal page code).
limits: Assumes the prior is flat across the interval and F(x,theta) is close to F(theta). The page warns the simplifications can fail.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete per-parameter price for complexity. A claim must earn its extra parameters in saved data bits.

source: Allison, MML Inference page (coin examples)
finding: Three coin tosses with one head tell us almost nothing about bias. Thirty tosses with 10 heads support suspecting a bias, about 0.2 < p < 0.4. Over-precise estimates are a form of over-fitting.
numbers: Examples: 1 head in 3 tosses; 10 heads in 30 tosses; a 9th-degree polynomial through 10 points is called almost certainly ridiculous.
limits: Teaching examples, not experiments.
agent_relevance: Do not state confidence digits that the sample size cannot support.

source: Allison, Strict MML page
finding: Strict MML (Wallace and Boulton 1975) maps data space to estimates so as to minimise expected two-part length. It is invariant and consistent. It is NP-hard in general. A polynomial algorithm exists for the binomial (Farr and Wallace 1997, 2002). Wallace-Freeman MML is the feasible approximation.
numbers: Farr and Wallace, Computer Journal 45(3):285-292, 2002.
limits: Secondhand through the Allison page. Original proofs not read.
agent_relevance: Exact optimal compression is intractable. Any scaffold use is an approximation with failure cases.

source: Wikipedia, Minimum message length (consistency claims)
finding: MML is described as statistically consistent, including on Neyman-Scott problems (data per parameter bounded above) and factor analysis, where plain maximum likelihood is inconsistent.
numbers: Neyman-Scott 1948; Dowe and Wallace 1997; Wallace and Dowe 1999 link to Kolmogorov complexity; Dowe, Gardner and Oppy 2007 (Br J Philos Sci 58(4):709-754). No simulation numbers in the page.
limits: Encyclopedia summary. The Dowe and Wallace 1997 paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: A code-length criterion can beat likelihood when each hypothesis has few data points, as in few-shot reasoning.

source: Wikipedia, MML history and relation to MDL
finding: MDL is described as developed about 10 years after MML with a possibly different, non-Bayesian motivation. MML was applied to decision trees (Needham and Dowe 2001) and Bayesian networks (Comley and Dowe 2003, 2005).
limits: Priority framing is the page's own. Allison says MML favours explicit priors, unlike MDL.
agent_relevance: Background only. Treat MML and MDL as near-equivalent scoring ideas.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum description length revisited
finding: Modern MDL review treats MML as a precursor or alternative. Its centre is universal codes: normalized maximum likelihood and the switch distribution. The switch distribution combines almost the best of AIC and BIC.
numbers: MML cited once as a precursor [Wallace and Boulton 1968]. AIC-BIC dilemma: AIC predicts better, BIC is consistent.
limits: I read the intro and section 3.1 text only. No MML versus MDL head-to-head numbers.
agent_relevance: Model selection by code length has known tradeoffs. The choice of code matters more than the label.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The description length of deep learning models
finding: Two-part codes with float32 weights are far worse than a uniform code. Variational codes also compress poorly. Simple prequential (online) coding compresses best.
numbers: Two-part float32: 1M params = 32 Mbits, about 200x the CIFAR10 uniform code. MNIST uniform 199 kbits. MNIST variational 24.1 kbits (ratio 0.12, 95.5% test acc). MNIST prequential 4.10 kbits (ratio 0.021, 99.5% acc). CIFAR10 variational 89.0 kbits (ratio 0.54, 61.6% acc). CIFAR10 prequential 45.3 kbits (ratio 0.27, about 93% acc).
limits: Image classification only. Explicit parameter codes (the MML style) lose badly for neural nets.
agent_relevance: Prefer an online predictive cost, like in-context learning, over explicit hypothesis-cost coding for big models.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) boundary condition
finding: Choosing a model by best variational code length gave worse test accuracy than standard training. Shortest description alone picked models that were too small.
numbers: Best variational-code model: MNIST 95.5% test accuracy, CIFAR10 61.6%. Prequential best-compression models: 99.5% and about 93%.
limits: Selection was by compression only. Not matched for size.
agent_relevance: Do not use compression as the only selector for a plan or claim.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language modeling is compression
finding: Chinchilla 70B, trained mainly on text, compresses other modalities better than domain compressors. Once model size is charged (a two-part code), large models only win on very large data.
numbers: Raw: ImageNet patches 43.4% vs PNG 58.5%; LibriSpeech 16.4% vs FLAC 30.3%; enwik9 Chinchilla 70B 8.3%. Adjusted for model size: Chinchilla 70B enwik9 21.9%, ImageNet 185.3%, LibriSpeech 228.9%; gzip enwik9 32.3%.
limits: Offline setting. Authors ignore model size when data is effectively infinite. Adjusted column read from pdftotext layout and may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: Two-part accounting says a huge model is justified only when reused on lots of data. Useful for judging scaffold complexity against gain.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) scaling side result
finding: With model size charged, bigger models give better adjusted rates on larger datasets but worse on small ones. There is a critical model size per dataset.
numbers: Transformers with 200K, 800K and 3.2M parameters trained on enwik8. Raw enwik9 rates 30.9%, 21.7%, 17.0%.
limits: Small vanilla transformers only. The adjusted curve is in a figure.
agent_relevance: This is the MML trade-off of parameter cost versus data fit, seen in practice. It supports adding machinery only when data justify it.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) boundary condition
finding: Transformers trained on enwik8 compress enwik9 well but not images, audio or random bytes. Random data cannot be compressed; gzip gives 100.0% on random data.
numbers: gzip on random data 100.0%. Random-data raw rates for Chinchilla models were above 195% in the table text.
limits: Table extraction is messy. Use the paper's table for exact values.
agent_relevance: Noise cannot be compressed. A rule that explains noise should be penalised.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-context learning and Occam's razor
finding: Next-token loss in in-context learners equals prequential code length, which rewards both fit and low model complexity. Meta-trained prequential ICL generalised better than train-risk ICL.
numbers: Generalisation gap (train-risk ICL minus prequential ICL) is positive at all task dimensionalities. It is largest in low-data regimes and grows with task difficulty. Polynomial tasks: meta-dataset of 10000 tasks of 2000 points each, 80/20 split. Also Mastermind and HMM tasks.
limits: Prequential coding is a near cousin of MML, not the same code. Small purpose-trained transformers plus one GPT-4 probe.
agent_relevance: In-context reasoning can act like an Occam prior. A compression-based way to judge in-context learning.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) GPT-4 on Mastermind
finding: GPT-4 failed to reduce prequential code length on a novel task. It did worse than a small transformer meta-trained on Mastermind tasks and worse than a naive baseline of the context's label frequencies.
numbers: Cross-entropy; error bars are standard error over 5 seeds. GPT-4 code length above the naive baseline.
limits: One task and one large model. Next-token loss alone does not guarantee low code length.
agent_relevance: A strong LLM can fail to compress a new rule from examples. Check rules by predicting held-out examples, not by how fluent they sound.

source: Voita and Titov (2020) Information-theoretic probing with MDL
finding: Probe accuracy can mislead. Description length (data plus model cost) separates real linguistic structure from memorised random labels without tuning probe size.
numbers: Control-task codelengths at least 2x the linguistic task. At layer 0 the control task has higher accuracy but about twice the codelength. Embedding-layer codelength about 2x that of layer 1.
limits: Probing of ELMo/BERT-style representations. Uses online and variational codes, not the Wallace-Freeman formula.
agent_relevance: Score a claim by both accuracy and the effort needed to reach it. A check against rationalisation.

source: Voita and Titov (2020) boundary condition
finding: Earlier probes needed small probe size or less training data to separate trained from random baselines. MDL probing separates them without those settings.
numbers: Online and variational codelengths show similar trends. The random-label task needs a model several times larger.
limits: The authors' own claim. Later critiques not read.
agent_relevance: If a check works only after tuning, it is weak. Code length is steadier.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression represents intelligence linearly
finding: Across 31 public LLMs and 12 benchmarks, average benchmark score is almost linear in bits per character on external text.
numbers: Pearson about -0.93 overall (RMSE 3.1%) and about -0.95 per domain (knowledge, coding, math). The correlation saturates at about 3M characters of corpus.
limits: Base models only. Short to medium contexts. May not hold where the ability has not emerged. Correlation across models, not a within-model test.
agent_relevance: Compression is a cheap unsupervised proxy for capability. It ranks base models; it does not test a scaffold.

source: Huang et al. (2024) outliers and limits
finding: Models scoring above the linear fit were flagged as likely overfit to the benchmark. Fine-tuned models are not valid general compressors.
numbers: Three stated limitations: base models only, short-to-medium context, well-trained models only.
limits: Outlier detection is by residual, so it is suggestive.
agent_relevance: Gap between compression and score can flag contamination.

source: Bornschein, Li and Hutter (2022) Sequential learning of neural networks for prequential MDL
finding: Online learning with rehearsal beats block-wise estimation for prequential description lengths. Forward-calibration helps. Reported description lengths improve on earlier results by large margins.
numbers: Table covers MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet with VGG++, WRN-28-10, ResNet-50 and others. I did not extract a before-after figure.
limits: I read the abstract, intro and table fragments only. Image classification only.
agent_relevance: Code-length measurement depends on the estimation procedure, so any compression-based check has method variance.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) Learning universal predictors
finding: Networks trained on data from random programs on universal Turing machines learn universal prediction strategies. Larger models do better. Transformer-L and LSTM-L match the optimal CTW predictor on variable-order Markov sources.
numbers: Architectures: RNN, LSTM, Stack-RNN, Tape-RNN, Transformer. LSTMs generalised to longer sequences (1024 steps) in the paper's plots.
limits: The simplicity prior is built into the training data, and it is Solomonoff-style, not MML. Synthetic sequences.
agent_relevance: An explicit simplicity prior in training data can induce Occam-like prediction. A scaffold cannot add that prior by prompting alone.

source: Allison, MML normal-distribution estimator
finding: For a normal sample, the page code's MML sigma estimate uses the N/(N-1) factor, matching the unbiased estimate rather than the divide-by-N ML estimate.
numbers: Code: s = sqrt((sumSq/N - mu^2) * N/(N-1)). ML: sumSq/N - mu^2.
limits: Toy implementation with range limits on mu and sigma. Not the full MML formula.
agent_relevance: Small-sample correction against overconfident variance, like caution about few-shot certainty.

source: Allison, Snob clustering note
finding: Wallace and Boulton's normal and multistate clustering work is described as one of the first uses of MML in a working machine-learning program, Snob. A 1998 special issue marked its 30th anniversary.
numbers: Computer Journal 41(8), 1998, special issue on clustering and classification.
limits: Page note only. No clustering accuracy figures.
agent_relevance: Historical use: clustering with the number of clusters chosen by message length.

source: Allison, KL-distance page
finding: KL divergence equals the expected extra message length per datum from using the wrong code. It is non-negative and asymmetric.
numbers: KL(p,q) = sum p_i log2(p_i/q_i); KL(p,p) = 0.
limits: Definition only.
agent_relevance: Links a wrong model to extra bits, which every compression-based check relies on.

source: Gap: MML-specific replication record
finding: I found no independent large replication or failed replication of MML itself. The arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned rate-limit errors and the web search budget was used up.
numbers: Zero MML-specific effect sizes obtained. Wallace and Freeman 1987, Dowe-Gardner-Oppy 2007 and Baxter and Oliver 1995 were not opened.
limits: This is a retrieval gap, not evidence of absence. A later pass should open Dowe 2010 and Baxter and Oliver 1995.
agent_relevance: Treat MML as a scoring theory, not a tested intervention. Nothing here measures it on LLM reasoning.

source: Gap: LLM studies naming MML
finding: Every LLM paper I opened uses MDL, prequential or Kolmogorov language. None names minimum message length. Grep of Elmoznino, Voita and Grau-Moya found no MML or Wallace hits.
numbers: MML or Wallace hits: 0 in Elmoznino, Voita, Grau-Moya; one mention in Grunwald and Roos.
limits: Grep ran on pdftotext output and could miss hyphenation. The Deletang PDF text was flagged binary, so that grep is not conclusive.
agent_relevance: MML is background for LLM work. No evidence it adds value beyond MDL-style checks.

source: Competing view: MML versus MDL on priors
finding: The stated difference: MML uses explicit priors and fully parameterised models. MDL uses universal codes without a prior. Grunwald and Roos describe the MDL side.
numbers: No head-to-head performance numbers in either source.
limits: Each camp's own description. Neutral comparisons not opened.
agent_relevance: Choose the code by practicality. Online codes won in neural nets and explicit two-part costs lost (Blier and Ollivier).
